extracted.intended_audience: IRB administrators, institutional officials, researchers conducting human subjects research, legal scholars, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_short: IRB review standards for human subjects research
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes regulatory and practical criteria governing Institutional Review Board (IRB) review under the Common Rule, including definitions of covered activities/subjects, levels of review, informed consent and risk–benefit requirements, and institutional implementation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk–benefit approval standard (45 C.F.R. §46.111(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[R]isks to subjects are reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits, if any, to subjects, and the importance of the knowledge that may reasonably be expected to result."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the legal standard IRBs must apply when approving studies. The Article emphasizes that IRB decisions hinge on this risk–benefit analysis and that both critics who accuse IRBs of under- and over-regulating focus on this standard. The text discusses difficulties in correctly determining a single risk–benefit profile for all prospective participants (see heterogeneity and aggregation problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Informed consent disclosure requirements (45 C.F.R. §46.116)
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs must ensure that recruitment materials and information disclosures "fully, accurately, and in 'understandable' language disclose to prospective participants, inter alia, 'any reasonably foreseeable risks or discomforts to [them]' and 'any benefits to [them] or to others which may reasonably be expected from the research.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs review recruitment plans, consent forms, and protocols before recruitment. The Article highlights the centrality of clear disclosure to voluntary informed consent and linkage of disclosures to the IRB's risk–benefit assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'research' (45 C.F.R. §46.102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Research" is defined as 'a systematic investigation . . . designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes uncertainty and controversy about when activities (e.g., piloting instruments, quality improvement, case studies) are 'systematic' or 'generalizable,' leading to regulatory gray areas that expand IRB scope. This definitional vagueness affects which activities fall under IRB oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'human subject' (45 C.F.R. §46.102(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Human subject" means a living individual about whom an investigator obtains data through intervention or interaction, or identifiable private information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations' definitions of intervention and interaction are broad (including environmental manipulation and communication), and uncertainty about what constitutes 'human subjects' sometimes complicates determinations of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-tiered review structure (full, expedited, exempt)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Common Rule categorizes HSR into three levels: default full IRB review, ten categories eligible for expedited review, and six categories exempt from review (45 C.F.R. provisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice these tiers often 'collapse' upward: IRBs commonly subject exemptible and expeditable research to expedited or full review. Surveys and reports cited show many institutions rarely grant exemptions; many IRBs will review nearly all protocols at full board meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited review eligibility and 'minimal risk' requirement (45 C.F.R. §46.110)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is eligible for expedited review if it imposes 'no more than minimal risk' and falls within one of the Secretary's ten specified categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs — not investigators — determine whether a protocol is expeditable and whether it involves 'no more than minimal risk.' The expedited reviewer (e.g., IRB chair or designee) can approve or require changes, but rejection must be sent to the full IRB. Empirical evidence indicates many expeditable studies still receive full review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt research and exemption determination procedures (45 C.F.R. §46.101(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Six categories of research are exempt from IRB review under the regulations, but the regulations do not specify who decides exemption status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPRR guidance (1995) advised that investigators should not have authority to make exemption decisions and should check with the IRB or designated authority. By practice, most institutions require investigators to submit protocols so the IRB can determine exemption status, and IRBs may nonetheless review exemptible research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Federal Wide Assurance (FWA) and institutional scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions engaged in federally funded HSR must file a Federal Wide Assurance promising to adhere to the regulations; the standard FWA invites institutions to apply the regulations to all HSR in which the institution is 'engaged.' (45 C.F.R. §46.103)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most institutions (historically 74%–90%) agree to extend the Common Rule campus-wide, which in practice brings most academic HSR under IRB review even if not federally funded. Many journals and contracts also effectively require IRB approval for publication or funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRB review duties prior to recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recruitment, IRBs review recruitment plans, detailed information disclosures (for informed consent), and the research protocol itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs ensure materials disclose foreseeable risks and benefits in understandable language and consider the protocol's risks and expected benefits when applying the risk–benefit standard; this front-loaded review is a key procedural duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of covered actors, activities, disciplines, and methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Common Rule and institutional practice cover a broad array of actors (academic institutions, contractors), activities (biomedical, social sciences, quality improvement, public policy experiments), disciplines (sociology, economics, history, law), and methods (drug trials, surveys, interviews, existing data analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of broad definitions and institutional extension via FWAs and publishing norms, IRB oversight reaches far beyond biomedical research and affects knowledge production across many fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk–benefit analysis process (three-step framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the regulatory standard an IRB must: (1) determine the magnitude of research-related harms and benefits and the value of the knowledge to be produced; (2) discount these (dis)utilities by their probabilities; and (3) determine whether the resulting risks to participants are 'reasonable in relation to' aggregate expected benefits to participants and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article emphasizes technical aspects: regulators treat probability differently for participant harms (discount by probability) and knowledge value (count only knowledge 'reasonably expected' to result). This formal framing exposes informational and aggregation difficulties for IRBs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information/central-planner problem (limits on IRB knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs assess risks and benefits before individual prospective participants are identified and therefore lack access to local, participant-specific information about preferences and circumstances necessary to predict how participation will affect individual welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article characterizes this as a 'classic central planner’s problem' and argues it undermines IRBs' ability to determine a meaningful single risk–benefit profile for all prospective participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation problem (single-study profile vs participant heterogeneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because prospective participants differ in susceptibilities and preferences, a study may pose low risk for some, high risk for others, and varying expected benefits; IRBs must nonetheless assign a single risk–benefit profile and judge its reasonableness for all prospective participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aggregation challenge complicates regulatory compliance and explains why IRBs may default to conservative, risk-averse decisions that may not align with many participants' preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory vagueness and IRB risk aversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague regulatory terms (e.g., 'research,' 'generalizable,' 'minimal risk') combined with IRBs' institutional incentives and attitudes tend to lead IRBs to err toward more rather than less review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article cites empirical findings and commentary showing many IRBs 'define up' research into higher scrutiny levels and that ambiguous terms contribute to conservative decisionmaking, increasing administrative costs and potential overregulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global reach of U.S. HSR regulations via FDA/Common Rule influence
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. regulations apply directly to research conducted or funded by Common Rule agencies outside the U.S.; foreign researchers seeking FDA market approval or to publish in U.S. journals must often comply with equivalent regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes that many countries have modeled their HSR protections on U.S. regulations and that journal and market incentives extend U.S. regulatory norms internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical institutional practices that expand IRB oversight (journals, contracts, policies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond statutory mandates, contractual relationships, employment policies, and journal submission requirements commonly extend IRB review to faculty and student HSR, and many institutions formally require submission of protocols for exemption determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: many journals require IRB approval for publication; FWAs and institutional policies bring non-federally funded research under IRB purview; surveys indicate widespread institutional extension of review to most campus research.
